intro: The **Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)** is the most-used questionnaire in clinical research to assess sleep quality. This simplified version evaluates **key components**: latency (how long you take to fall asleep), duration, efficiency, disturbances, and subjective quality. A global score >5 indicates poor sleep quality.
keyTakeaway: **PSQI ≤5**: good sleep quality. **PSQI >5**: poor sleep quality. Components: latency (min to fall asleep), efficiency (% of time in bed sleeping), duration, and disturbances.
useCases: You sleep poorly and want an objective assessment of your sleep quality.
Your doctor asked for a sleep questionnaire as screening.

You suspect sleep quality affects your performance.
You track your sleep quality monthly.

fields.label: How do you rate your sleep overall?
Do you have daytime sleepiness or low energy?

faq.a: **5 or less** indicates good sleep quality. **More than 5** indicates poor quality. Maximum score is 21 (worst possible quality).

faq.q: How many minutes is normal to fall asleep?
faq.a: **10-20 minutes** is normal. Less than 5 can indicate extreme sleep deprivation. More than 30 minutes is considered **sleep-onset insomnia**.
It's the percentage of time in bed you actually sleep. **>85%** is good efficiency. If you spend 8 hours in bed but only sleep 5, your efficiency is 62.5% (poor).

faq.q: Is waking up at night normal?
faq.a: 1-2 brief awakenings are normal. If you wake **3+ times** or take over 20 min to fall back asleep, it may indicate a sleep disorder.
If your PSQI is **>10**, if you have insomnia 3+ nights per week for over 3 months, or if you snore loudly with daytime sleepiness (possible apnea).

faq.q: Does this test detect sleep apnea?
faq.a: **Not directly.** PSQI measures general quality. If you have loud snoring, breathing pauses, and excessive daytime sleepiness, you need a sleep study (polysomnography).

faq.q: How to improve my PSQI score?
faq.a: **Fixed schedule** (sleep and wake at same time), **no screens 1h before**, **cool and dark bedroom**, **no caffeine after 2pm**, **regular exercise** (not at night).

explanation:
## What Is the PSQI

The **Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)** was developed by **Buysse et al. (1989)** at the University of Pittsburgh and is the world's most-cited questionnaire for assessing subjective sleep quality over the **previous 4 weeks**. It appears in over 3,000 peer-reviewed studies and has been validated in more than 30 languages. It evaluates **7 components**: subjective quality, latency, duration, efficiency, disturbances, medication use, and daytime dysfunction. Each component scores 0 to 3; global score goes from **0 to 21**. Higher score = worse sleep.

## How the Score Is Calculated

Each of the 7 components is scored from 0 (no difficulty) to 3 (severe difficulty) based on your answers:

| Component | What it measures |
|---|---|
| C1 — Subjective quality | Your own rating of sleep quality |
| C2 — Sleep latency | How long it takes to fall asleep + how often you struggle |
| C3 — Sleep duration | Actual hours of sleep (not time in bed) |
| C4 — Sleep efficiency | Hours slept ÷ hours in bed × 100 |
| C5 — Sleep disturbances | Frequency of 9 common disruptions (pain, cold, heat, etc.) |
| C6 — Sleep medication | How often you use any sleep aid |
| C7 — Daytime dysfunction | Trouble staying awake + loss of enthusiasm |

The **global PSQI score** is the sum of all 7 component scores (0–21). This simplified calculator approximates that total; the full clinical version requires the original 19-item questionnaire available from the University of Pittsburgh.

## Score Interpretation

| Score | Category | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 – 4 | Good quality | Restorative sleep |
| 5 | Cutoff | Suggests follow-up |
| 6 – 10 | Poor quality | Habit changes recommended |
| 11 – 15 | Very poor | Doctor consultation recommended |
| 16 – 21 | Severe | Possible disorder — refer to specialist |

The **cutoff of 5** yields a sensitivity of 89.6% and specificity of 86.5% for distinguishing good from poor sleepers (Buysse et al., 1989). This is the most validated threshold in clinical research.

## Key Components Explained

- **Sleep efficiency**: hours slept ÷ hours in bed × 100. **≥85%** is considered healthy. Efficiency below 75% is a core criterion for clinical insomnia.
- **Sleep latency**: normal range is **10–20 minutes**. Under 5 minutes may indicate severe sleep deprivation or a sleep disorder; over 30 minutes consistently points to sleep-onset insomnia.
- **Sleep duration**: The National Sleep Foundation recommends **7–9 hours** for adults (18–64 years) and **7–8 hours** for adults 65+. Consistently sleeping under 6 hours is associated with increased risk of metabolic and cardiovascular disease in prospective cohort studies.
- **Daytime dysfunction** is often the most underrated component: falling asleep unintentionally or losing motivation during the day carries independent health implications beyond nighttime symptoms.

## What the PSQI Does NOT Cover

Understanding the limits of this tool prevents misuse:

- **Does not diagnose sleep apnea.** OSA (obstructive sleep apnea) requires polysomnography or a validated home sleep test. Red flags: loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, morning headaches, or waking unrefreshed despite 8+ hours in bed.
- **Does not detect circadian rhythm disorders** (e.g., delayed sleep phase syndrome), which require actigraphy over multiple weeks.
- **Does not differentiate insomnia subtypes** (onset vs. maintenance vs. early awakening) — relevant for treatment decisions.
- **Does not replace clinical diagnosis.** A PSQI ≥5 is a screening flag, not a diagnosis.

## Common Mistakes When Completing the PSQI

- **Confusing "time in bed" with "time asleep."** C4 (efficiency) depends on this distinction. If you lie in bed for 9 hours but sleep only 6.5, your efficiency is ~72% — clinically poor.
- **Averaging unusual weeks.** The PSQI asks about the *last month*. One bad night inflates the score; one vacation week deflates it. Answer based on your typical pattern.
- **Ignoring medication use.** Over-the-counter antihistamines (diphenhydramine), melatonin supplements, and alcohol used as sleep aids all count in C6. Underreporting this component is frequent.
- **Not counting wakeful time.** If you wake at 3 a.m. for 45 minutes, that subtracts from your sleep duration even if you eventually fall back asleep.

## Factors That Move Your Score

- **Sleep hygiene** — consistent schedule, bedroom at ~18 °C / 65 °F, blackout curtains, and no screens 1 hour before bed — has been shown in controlled studies to reduce PSQI scores by 2–4 points.
- **Caffeine**: has a half-life of ~5–6 hours. A 3 p.m. coffee still has 50% of its stimulant effect at 8–9 p.m., directly increasing latency and reducing deep sleep (N3 stage).
- **Alcohol**: accelerates sleep onset (hence the misperception that it "helps"), but suppresses REM sleep and causes rebound wakefulness in the second half of the night — worsening C5 and C7.
- **Exercise**: regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with improved PSQI scores, but intense training within 2–3 hours of bedtime can delay sleep onset in sensitive individuals.

## Complementing the PSQI With Objective Data

The PSQI is entirely self-reported, which is both its strength (accessible, no equipment) and its limitation. Wearables such as **Oura Ring** or **Whoop** provide continuous heart rate variability and estimated sleep stage data that can reveal discrepancies between perceived and actual sleep — useful if your subjective score seems inconsistent with how you feel daily. Neither device, however, replaces clinical polysomnography for diagnosing disorders.
